anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite reasonably accurate statistics, causing excessive I/O, CPU, or memory consumption per statement.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long wait chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions accumulate faster than background cleanup can purge them, inflating table and index size and adding visibility-check overhead.

When all three root causes strike at once, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: expensive plans run far longer than expected, keeping row, page, or metadata locks open; these prolonged locks block other transactions, generating extensive wait chains and frequent deadlock rollbacks; while the blocking persists, update and delete activity continues to create new MVCC versions that cannot be reclaimed because readers are still attached to old snapshots and writers are stalled behind locks. Operators observe high CPU from poor plans, rising lock-wait time and deadlock reports, steadily growing table size, bloated indexes, widening gaps between planner estimates and actual row counts, and dramatic drops in overall transaction throughput coupled with surging application-level timeouts.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan often performs wide table scans or nested-loop explosions that touch many more rows than necessary, enlarging the lock footprint and lock duration. The resulting blocking keeps transactions open, preventing vacuum/cleanup workers from advancing the version horizon; this accelerates MVCC bloat. In turn, the swollen heap and indexes skew the optimizer’s cost calculations, making it even more likely to choose poor plans for subsequent compilations. The larger on-disk structures also lengthen lock hold times for index or page-level locks, intensifying contention. Meanwhile, the backlog of obsolete versions elevates I/O and CPU pressure, slowing both foreground statements and background cleaners, further aggravating plan quality and lock congestion in a self-reinforcing loop.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the timeout in seconds for attempts to acquire metadata locks.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_wait_timeout while attempting to acquire a metadata lock.
entry.workload_impact: The metadata lock acquisition fails and the statement does not proceed.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
